summary:
This A/B run covered 8 investigation-style WAF/incident-RCA evals (one, negative-unrelated-rds, was skipped since it is a should-not-trigger case — trigger correctly did not require investigation, so no meaningful comparison there). Across the remaining 7 evals, trigger_fired was 100% for both variants in every eval, so the behavior-under-test reliably activated regardless of variant.

Expected-output match (did the overall output meet the expected outcome) favored with_skill in most evals: with_skill hit 100% in 5 of 7 evals and 67% in the other 2 (e5, e7 context differs — in e7 without_skill actually scored 100% vs with_skill's 67%, a reversal). In contrast, without_skill matched expected output poorly in several evals — 0% in e2 (injection-browser-ua) and e4 (detected-not-blocked-rate-rule), 67% in e3, e5, e6, and 100% only in e7. These expected-output judgments were generally made with high confidence, so this is a reasonably solid signal, though e7's reversal shows the pattern isn't universal.

Per-assertion pass rates follow the same general lean: with_skill's assertion pass rates ranged from 39%-81% across evals, while without_skill's ranged from 7%-61%, with with_skill ahead in 6 of 7 evals and roughly comparable in e5 (39% vs 42%). Importantly, several individual assertions passed for neither variant (e.g., the root-cause mitigation-separation assertion in e3, the scoped rate-rule recommendation in e4), indicating those specific expected behaviors are hard for both variants or the assertions need refinement. Other assertions passed for both consistently (e.g., naming conventions in e1, e7's Gaps/Web-ACL assertions), meaning they don't differentiate the variants. A few assertions showed a clean split where with_skill passed and without_skill failed across all runs (e.g., card-testing detection in e4, security-group root cause and supporting evidence in e6), which are more informative signals than the aggregate percentages alone.

Quality comparisons (pairwise LLM judgments across accuracy/evidence criteria) were skipped entirely for e2 and e4 (no pairs evaluated), so no quality signal exists there. Where evaluated, with_skill was favored more often in e1, e3, e6, e7 (ranging from 6-9 favorable judgments vs 0-2 for without_skill), while without_skill was favored more often in e5 (6 vs 0, with 2 comparable). Confidence on these quality judgments was mostly high to medium.

Runtime and cost showed a mixed, non-decisive pattern: with_skill was slower and more expensive in e1, e2, e3, e6, e7 (differences of roughly 2-7 minutes and $1-$3), while without_skill was slower/costlier in e4 (slightly) and comparable in e3. Context-window utilization was consistently lower for without_skill across all evals (roughly half or less of with_skill's), though this didn't translate into a consistent quality advantage.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was similar for both variants overall, mostly landing in "mostly_consistent," with e2 showing both variants as "inconsistent" (with_skill slightly less inconsistent) and e6 showing without_skill as "inconsistent" while with_skill was "mostly_consistent." Some output_consistency data was missing entirely (with_skill in e3, without_skill in e5), limiting how much can be concluded there.

Overall, with_skill tended to meet expected outputs and pass assertions more often, and was favored in quality judgments in most evals, but it also typically ran longer and cost more, and used more context window. Variant_b was faster, cheaper, and lower-context-usage, and outperformed on expected-output and quality in e5 and on expected-output in e7, with assertion rates roughly on par with with_skill there. Several specific assertions failed for both variants, highlighting gaps in current behavior independent of which variant is used, and the quality comparison having zero evaluated pairs in two evals means part of the picture is simply missing rather than favoring either side.

e1-two-false-positives-one-window.summary:
Both variants fired the trigger in all 3 runs and both met the top-level "expected output" criterion in all 3 runs with high confidence, so at that coarse level the two are equivalent.

Where they diverge is in the detailed assertion checks (18 assertions across 3 runs each): with_skill passed 14/18 (78%) vs without_skill's 10/18 (56%). Looking assertion-by-assertion rather than at the aggregate:
- Two assertions passed for both variants at or near 100% ("names both sub-rules" and "supporting observations cite log/metric evidence") — these aren't discriminating between the variants.
- One assertion ("separate Cause records per sub-rule with counts/time windows") failed for both variants (with_skill 0/3, without_skill 1/3) — this indicates the behavior itself is weak across both agents, not a point in either's favor.
- Three assertions showed a clear gap favoring with_skill: classifying both sub-rule matches as false positives (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 1/3), explicitly ruling out a WAF config change as root cause (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 2/3), and confirming no managed-rule-version change occurred (with_skill 2/3 vs without_skill 0/3). All of these judgments were rated high confidence, so this pattern is a reasonably solid signal, not noise.

The pairwise quality comparison (3 pairs, high avg confidence) also leans toward with_skill: 9 of 12 scored sub-criteria favored with_skill, 2 favored without_skill, 1 was comparable. Variant_a was favored consistently on "key findings accuracy" (3/3) and "root cause accuracy" (2/3, 1 comparable), with a more mixed picture on "impact analysis accuracy" and "supporting evidence quality" (2-1 splits each). This is a small sample (only 3 pairs), so the direction is suggestive rather than conclusive.

On cost and speed, with_skill was faster (avg ~14m19s vs ~16m54s) and cheaper (avg $7.13 vs $8.42), while using more of its context window (13.2% vs 6.7%, no compaction for either). The separate runtime-threshold comparison (3 pairs, only 1 run exceeding a 30s threshold) carries low average confidence, so little weight should be put on that specific figure.

Output consistency across repeated runs was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants, with with_skill scoring marginally higher (2.5 vs 2.0 on the internal scale, medium confidence for both) — a small, low-certainty difference.

Overall, this is a case where the two variants agree on the broad pass/fail outcome but with_skill shows a consistent edge on several specific, high-confidence assertions and on pairwise quality judgments, while also running somewhat faster and cheaper in this sample. One shared weak spot (the two-separate-Cause-records requirement) suggests a common area needing improvement regardless of variant. Given the small number of runs (3) underlying every comparison, these directional differences should be read as a current snapshot rather than a definitive gap.

Output A's 'root cause' section conflates the proximate cause (which rules blocked) with root cause but doesn't clearly distinguish 'no config change' as a separate, explicit finding, nor does it explicitly frame the structural reason (default Block mode + structural sub-rule limits) as the fundamental cause. Output B has a dedicated '### Root Cause' section that explicitly states the fundamental cause: CommonRuleSet runs in default Block mode with structural sub-rules misclassifying legitimate traffic, confirms via CloudTrail that no config change occurred, and explicitly states that input change (traffic pattern) is what triggered it. This is a more rigorous and complete root cause articulation, correctly distinguishing the trigger (traffic/input change) from the structural root cause (default rule configuration).

Output B provides three distinct, well-organized findings: (1) no config change (ruling out a regression hypothesis with explicit CloudTrail evidence across multiple event types), (2) the specific CRS sub-rules responsible with precise block counts and client IP counts, and (3) an explicit root cause tying it together with the structural/default-mode framing. Output A's findings section is a single blended finding that includes the no-config-change point as a passing remark ('No WAF/CloudFront config change occurred (CloudTrail)') without giving it the weight or detail of a separate, evidenced finding. Output B's structure and content show deeper, more systematic contributing-factor analysis.

Output A has a detailed Supporting Observations section with specific CloudWatch metric correlation (BlockedRequests series matching Rule=ALL), phase timing, and baseline comparisons (same-day and prior-day), which is strong evidence. Output B lacks an explicit '#### Supporting Observations' subsection under its Cause/Root Cause headers, but compensates with specific evidence embedded directly in the Cause/Root Cause descriptions themselves (CloudTrail sweep details across many event types, specific client IPs, ALLOW traffic volume ~146,911 reqs, 2 clients) and a detailed Gaps section analyzing IP ownership ambiguity. Per the criteria instructions, the presence of a Supporting Observations section itself is evidence of better support, which favors Output A structurally; however, Output B's embedded evidence is arguably more specific and actionable (exact IPs, exact ALLOW traffic volumes, structured CloudTrail sweep across many event types). Weighing both, this is close, but Output A's explicit observational structure with phase-by-phase baseline comparison is slightly more rigorous as a dedicated evidence section, while Output B's lack of formal 'Supporting Observations' header is a structural shortfall. Given the instructions emphasize presence of such sections as evidence of quality, Output A edges out here — but Output B's gaps section and embedded evidence are also very strong. On balance, this is close enough to lean slightly to output_b due to richer embedded details (IP addresses, allow traffic context, CloudTrail breadth) even though it lacks the formal section header, but output_a's explicit structured observations with metric correlation are also compelling. I'll call this closer to equivalent leaning B due to specificity depth in root cause support, but A's dedicated section format is strong too.

e2-injection-browser-ua.summary:
This evaluation covers one investigation task (an incident RCA involving AWS WAF-blocked attack probes) run 3 times for each variant.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants (this was only tracked once, not per-variant).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence), while without_skill met it in none of its 3 runs (0/3, high confidence). This is a clear and high-confidence gap on the primary success criterion for this task.

Assertions: Aggregating across the 6 distinct assertion checks (each run 3 times = 18 checks), with_skill passed 14/18 (78%) and without_skill passed 4/18 (22%). Breaking this down:
- Three naming assertions (correctly naming the specific WAF rules SQLi_QUERYARGUMENTS, CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS, Log4JRCE_HEADER) were passed consistently by with_skill (3/3 each) but only intermittently by without_skill (1/3 each) — a notable and consistent gap, though without_skill's partial passes show the behavior isn't entirely absent.
- The assertion requiring exact WAF rule identifiers (not just generic labels) alongside the ~210 blocked count was passed 3/3 by with_skill and 1/3 by without_skill (both at high LLM-judge confidence).
- Two harder assertions — correctly flagging the ~15 allowed/missed-by-rule requests as a separate finding, and giving the correct overall root-cause assessment (correct mitigation but missed file-read residue, no rule-loosening recommendation) — were passed only 1/3 by with_skill and 0/3 by without_skill. These two assertions are essentially failing for both variants, indicating this is a difficult behavior that neither variant reliably achieves, rather than a case where one variant clearly outperforms the other.

Metrics: without_skill ran faster (10m2s vs 14m22s, about 4m20s less) and cheaper ($5.00 vs $7.16) than with_skill, and used less of its context window (4.7% vs 12.2%, with zero compaction for both). This is a real tradeoff: without_skill's lower cost/time runs alongside its lower pass rates and lower expected-output match rate.

Quality comparison: No head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, all 3 skipped), so there is no additional quality signal beyond the assertions and expected-output results.

Output consistency: Both variants were rated "inconsistent" overall across repeated runs. with_skill scored somewhat higher on the consistency scale (1.75, with 3 of 4 dimensions "mostly_consistent" and 1 "inconsistent", medium average confidence) than without_skill (1.25, with 1 "mostly_consistent" and 3 "inconsistent" dimensions, high average confidence). Both show meaningful run-to-run variability, with without_skill's variability somewhat more pronounced and measured with higher confidence.

Overall state: On the measured dimensions that could be directly compared, with_skill shows a consistently higher pass rate on expected output and most individual assertions (several at high confidence), while without_skill is faster, cheaper, and uses less context. Both variants struggle equally with the two most nuanced assertions (identifying the allowed/missed requests and giving the fully correct root-cause assessment), and both show some run-to-run inconsistency, with without_skill's being somewhat greater. No quality-comparison data is available to supplement these findings.
